2. At the outset the Chairman welc omed the Members to the sitting of the Committee and 
apprised them about the agenda of the meeting i.e. "issues related to safety of women". It was 
informed that apart from NGO's the Committee would also discuss the issue with the Ministry of 
Women and Child Development in the post lunch session. 
3. The Chairman then welcomed the representatives of Jagori, Centre for Social Research, All 
India Women's Conference and Multiple Action Research Group. The Chairman thereafter, 
requested the NGO's to share their experiences on the issue with the Committee and the legislative 
changes and other measures/steps that need to be introduced to check the anti -social elements and 
promote the safety of women. The Chairman also urged them to suggest innovative strategies to 
utilize the Nirbhaya Fund in a more pragmatic and effective manner. 
4. Chairperson, Jagori in her presentation stressed on the need to ensure overall  safety of 
women everywhere be it a college, a school, shopping complex, work place, home and so on. 
Differentiating between prevention of violence and response to violence, she  stressed upon issues 
like including women representatives in urban planning to ensure safe cities, safe transport, gender 
transformative budgeting, panic response and related issues.  
5. Executive Director, MARG in his presentation reiterated some of the issued highlighted by 
representatives of Jagori and stressed upon self -defence training and steps to boost the judicial 
process of women related cases and implementation of legal rights of women. He also stressed 
upon change of mindset and teach the boys to respect and empower women. 
6. Executive Director, Centre for Social Research in her presentation stressed on the issues 
related to dowry harassment, trafficking of women and children, marital rape, swiftness/surety  of 
punishment, setting up of special courts, implementing of Vishakha guidelines and related issues.  

55 
 
7. Representative of All India Women Conference in her briefing to the Committee stressed 
upon filling the vacancies of Judges, gender sensitization training of police personnel, setting up of  
forensic labs in the country, empowering women and inculcating values in the boys. She also 
highlighted the under utilisation of Nirbhaya Fund. 
8. The members then sought some clarifications from the witnesses and asked them to furnish 
their replies in writing. 
(The witnesses then withdrew) 
 
(The Committee re-assembled at 3:00 pm) 
9. The Chairman while welcoming the Special Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child 
Development expressed his satisfaction on the fact that representatives of different 
Ministries/Departments like Home Affairs, Railways, Road Transport and Highways and Justice 
had come for deliberation on the subject i.e. 'Issues relating to Safety of women' .  The Chairman, 
expressed his concern on the rising incidences of crime against women and sought the views of the 
Ministries/Departments present on the measures that need to be taken to curb this trend. He also 
sought to be briefed about the measures on which the Nirbhaya Fund could be utilized in an 
efficient and effective manner.  
10. Special Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development in his presentation briefed 
the Committee about the legal provisions contained in different Acts and the steps taken to make 
them more effective. The Committee was briefed about the poor status of utiliza tion of the 
Nirbhaya fund and the lack of response by a number of states. The Committee was also briefed 
about the steps taken by the Ministry of Home Affairs to ensure prevention of crimes against 
women and sensitize the police administration while dealin g with victims of gender based crime. 
Representatives of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and Railway Board also apprised the 
Committee about the steps taken to ensure safety of women. 
11. The representative of the Department of Justice submitted th at Fast Track Special Courts 
have been set up to deal with heinous crimes against women and cases under POCSO Act. The 
Committee was informed that 20 States/UTs out of 31 have joined the Fast Track Special Court

RECOMMENDATIONS  
 
The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and 
Sports examined the subject Preparation for Olympics – 2021. After exhaustive deliberations with all the 
concerned stakeholders the Committee recommends the following. 
 
1. Recovery from COVID impact 
a. Undertaking physiological, mental, and nutritional assessment of all athletes in the Olympics 
contingent to find strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and th reats in their preparation. Making 
it mandatory for athletes to undergo indepth cardio-pulmonary function tests to monitor recovery 
to top fitness level.  Also arranging for very scientific Musculo -skeletal rehab to original fitness 
to avoid injuries due t o sudden loads, specially at remote centers if athletes are not training at 
main centers.   
b. Providing athletes with support and training customised to the results of the assessment report 
card. 
c. Identifying the  training facilities, stadiums, and sports cent res for Olympic qualified athletes 
which have not opened yet. Re-open these centres at the earliest or relocatinc athletes to alternate 
centres which have opened. 
d. Due to lockdown and travel restrictions, there was loss of international/national competition  
exposure which has hugely affected the training of the athletes. The Department and NSFs must 
ensure that players get an opportunity to play maximum international tournaments before the 
2021 Olympic Games. International competitions should be accorded pri ority as they prepare 
athletes for pressure situations they may find themselves in during actual Olympics. 
e. It has been observed that travelling to far away tournaments is a big challenge for athletes. 
Besides, countries like France and Germany that host to urnaments at home, have produced more 
champions. India should host more international tournaments, so that players can reduce travel to 
collect more points and move up the ranking ladder. Also, a larger number of athletes can benefit 
from the same amount that India spends on sending athletes abroad for exposure. 
f. Due to the halting of domestic and international sporting competitions, athletes may not have 
experienced adequate competition in the run up to Olympics 2021. This need may be felt more 
severely in competitive sports, illustratively wrestling and badminton. It is important to identify 
and organise competitive matchups to give the necessary experience to the qualified athletes. 
2. Bio-Bubbles 
a. Creating bio -bubbles in the training facilities such that athletes can be isolated in a secure 
environment and train with minimal possibility of being infected. 

  
６ 
b. Using bio -bubbles for ensuring championship participation in games for athletes and 
sportspersons before the Olympics commence in foreign countries. 
c. Ensuring bio-bubbles for the Indian athletes and sportspersons at the Olympics. 
d. Giving individualized programs to athletes capable of reaching finals or medal hopefuls and also 
providing for sending them abroad as soon as possible in a bubble environment where  top 
scientific infrastructure is available. 
 
3. Institutional Support 
a. Swift decision making:  The government should be swift in making decisions and granting 
approvals, viz, financial grants, equipment, representation in international competitions, etc. to 
avoid unnecessary delays. GOI should be prepared in dealing smoothly and quickly with any 
unforeseen situations that may arise due to COVID. 
b. Selection process:  Qualification and selection of the olympic core probables should be 
completed on time. The selecti on schedule should be announced well in advance and the 
timeline should be adhered to. All efforts should be made to avoid any last minute selections. 
c. Coaches: 
i. Several foreign coaches resigned and returned to their respective countries in the course 
of the pandemic. Besides, most sporting disciplines have foreign experts who are either 
65 or above. Those above 65 were asked by their respective NSFs to not visit training 
venues. 
ii. About 561 vacancies exist of Coaches. This is unacceptable. These should be fill ed up 
within specific time-bound manner so that Olympic preparations don’t suffer. 
iii. Additionally, an immediate survey should be carried out in collaboration with the NSFs 
to gauge requirements for coaches, including personal coaches for athletes. 
iv. The Depart ment should lay out timelines to recruit vacancies for foreign experts and 
coaches. 
4. Human and Technical resource Support 
a. Appointing a chief procurement officer in the Mission Olympic Cell (MOC) created under the 
Chairmanship of the Director General, Sports  Authority (DG, SAI) as part of The Olympics 
Podium Scheme (TOPS) to coordinate and fast track procurement of training equipment which is 
in shortage. 

  
７ 
b. Asking head coaches to undertake a sports equipment availability analysis across their respective 
sporting facilities. Requests for essential equipment in shortage should be immediately escalated 
to the MOC who can fast track procurement and provisioning of the equipment. 
c. Governing bodies for respective sports like Wrestling Federation of India, National Rifl e 
Association of India, Hockey India can coordinate special training camps to concentrate training 
efforts for qualified athletes. 
d. Creating a dedicated digital portal for all athletes to list their equipment, training, and nutritional 
requirements. Fulfilment of these requirements can be centrally coordinated by the MOC, TOPS. 
e. Engaging professional sports performance analysis experts to assist in statistical  and data backed 
inputs to athletes on their performance and techniques. 
f. Engaging domestic ex-players, regularised sportspersons, as well as global experts/consultants in 
a virtual mode to guide preparations of the athletes in the final stages of preparation for 
Olympics 2021. 
g. Asking head coaches to create a customised 200 -day plan for every qualified athlete. The plan 
should list the focus areas for training, guidelines for preparation, and nutritional advice that 
athletes can follow to streamline their preparation. 
 
5. Medical& Doping 
a. Medical facilities : Medical staff and other medical equipment (like X -Ray and MRI) should be 
made available within select SAI and other training centres. This will ensure that athletes do not 
lose any time for treatment and recovery. This will also keep them from travelling to hospitals 
where the chances of contracting COVID are the highest. 
i. Dedicated physiotherapists should be made available in all the national training centres. 
b. Medical Insurance :  Sport injury insurance schemes should be put in place for sportspersons, 
through a collaborative framework by the central and state governments. The insurance schemes 
should be tailored as per the needs of each sports discipline, each state, and should cover players 
from different categories 
c. COVID-19 Vaccination : Athletes as well as coaches and support staff going for the Olympics 
should be put in the priority group for the vaccination process. 
d. Doping Sensitization:Regular webinars and e -learning courses should be organized to educate 
athletes and coaches about doping. 
e. World Anti-Doping Code :They should also be made aware of the changes in the 2021 World 
Anti-Doping Code. 

  
８ 
f. NADA as an independent body:  Expedite efforts to setup NADA as an autonomous body 
independent of government. 
g. National Anti -Doping Authority (NADA) helpline : They should have access to a full time 
functional National Anti-Doping Authority (NADA) helpline where they can seek advice in case 
of any doubt.It should be made clear to all the athletes that instances of doping will not be taken 
lightly. 
 
6. Corporate Sponsorship 
For the 2016 Rio Olympics, Indian Olympic Association (IOA) had signed up with a sport management 
firm and a huge amount as sponsorship was raised from the private and corporate sector. However, due to 
COVID, many NSFs have lost their sponsors this time  - as has been pointed out by IOA in their 
presentation to the Committee. It is suggested that IOA should sign up with a sponsorship management 
firm on an immediate basis for this edition of the Olympics as well, and try to rope in the private sector for 
funds. 
 
7. Women athletes 
a. Gender sensitization: Gender sensitization of all male athletes and coaches should be done to prevent 
incidences of sexist behaviour and sexual harassment. 
b. All schemes and incentives designed for the athletes should be gender neutral. 
c. Women should be encouraged to participate in as many sporting events as possible so that atleast 
50% of the Olympic contingent consists of women in the near future. 
 
8. Financial aid for athletes during their tenure as Sportspersons 
a. The committee recommends undertaking a National Olympic Scholarship Programme in a phased 
manner. It must guarantee minimum, but fixed financial aid to every athlete who does well at the 
national level. This funding needs to be scaled up as athletes begin to compete on the world stage. 
b. Private funding to individual athletes is still very low, as compared to other nations. Athletes should 
be trained to raise funds from private sources as well. Besides, incentives to donors and sponsors will 
also spur such private sector participation. 
 
9. Financial Security for medal winning athletes and their coaches during and post their sports 
careers 
a. The Ministry must place before the Standing Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth 
and Sports a formula at the earliest for ensuring financial security for medal winning athletes and 
their coaches during and post their sports careers. The Ministry must formulate such a formula 
based on the sportsperson and coach’s contribution to the Flag for the Sports. This formula must 

  
９ 
take care of financial security as mentioned above including consideration regarding stipends, 
jobs, post-retirements annuities, etc.  
b. There have been several instances of athletes not getting government jobs even after bringing 
medals in major international games. There should be an assured 3% sports quota reservation in 
government jobs for all the medal -winning athletes. For the p eriod of unemployment, the 
Department should grant easily accessible financial aid. 
c. The Ministry must give the cover of Life Insurance and Health Insurance to all Olympians as a 
mark of respect for their services to the country.  
10. Budgetary Allocation 
a. Increased allocation for TOPS programme: TOPS is being used as a top -up programme for 
covering discretionary expenses that NSFs cannot fund. This is unacceptable. TOPS as an 
independent programme should be reaffirmed and increased allocation for Olympic prepara tions 
should be made at the earliest.  
b. Stop practice of slashing “Support to NSF” funds:  It has become a practice to keep slashing 
funds in Revised Estimates (RE) as compared to Budgeted allocation under “Support to NSF”. 
This fund should not be seen as a soft target and funds slashed indiscriminately which affects 
Olympics preparations. 
 
11.  Best Practices 
a. Talent Spotting: In the identified Priority and High Priority Sports by the Ministry, the focus 
should be on talent spotting from the bottom -up, from the Panchayats, Blocks and Districts of 
India. Talent should be spotted from the School levels and nurtured to the Olympics level. 
b. Comparative analysis: of top medal winning Countries in these priority and high priority Sports 
and strategies employed by them in their: 
i. Talent Spotting 
ii. Training 
iii. Event-Day peaking and build-up for the Sportsperson and Athlete 
iv. Nutrition, Diet and Physio Support 
c. Ministry should work towards building world -class infrastructure and facilities as per 
international standards. A sincere a nd institutionalized effort should be made to ensure 
maintenance of the infrastructure so created. 
d. Training abroad: Focus should be on sending sportspersons and athletes for training abroad so 
that they have the best training at international standards of excellence. 

  
１０ 
e. Specialisation in Supporting Staff and their dedicated availability: To ensure that the 
Supporting Staff for the athletes and sportspersons have the requisite specialisation or are 
provided substantial training for improving their specialisatio n and their dedicated availability is 
ensured. 
f. There have been cases of high -performing players being excluded from the TOPS scheme. It is 
suggested to reassess the list, and create a wider net to include those deserving and left out from 
the TOPS list. 
g. Though the Department of Sports has already identified High priority Disciplines and Priority 
Disciplines based on winning potential, an outcome -oriented approach should be deployed in 
training of the athletes belonging to these disciplines. 
h. With the postponement of the games, India can gain from a bigger pool of athletes who could 
win an Olympic quota for the 2021 games. A transparent selection process, along with the 
calendar for each priority discipline should be laid out. 
i. States should recognise ‘s ports’ as an industry via their respective industrial policies to provide 
an impetus to the sector, and encourage investment in infrastructure development. This would 
open up opportunities for availing of subsidy, loan and assistance from private and gover nment 
sources. 
j. The Department should consider encouraging private investments in the sector. Current CSR 
contributions to sport only amount to about a paltry 2% of all CSR funds. Providing special 
incentives to invest in sports will aid in attracting the corporate world.

Action Taken 
The talent selection Process is as per the international best practices 
considering that the objective is to select best available talent. Therefore, a two -tier

Action Taken 
Noted for compliance. Also 
(i) Talent selection is the culling of players with the current ability to participate and  
be successful in events taking place in the near future. Talent identification, on the  
other hand, is the prediction of future performance based upon an  evaluation of  
current physical, technical, tactical and psychological qualities. Talent selection is  
simpler, but talent identification is an art. One yields great results to -day; the other  
builds elite athletes and winning teams for the future. 
(ii) Talent identification also takes a long term approach to selection and 
development and focuses on training large numbers of players, instead of pruning  
and selecting a few on the basis of current performance to win in near future.

Athletics, Football and Hockey. At present, the capacity of SAI Training Centres

REPLIES 
Observations/Recommendations 
That the Department should make concerted efforts in first utilizing the 
allocated funds rationally and then getting/mobilizing the adequate resources. It 
should approach private and corporate sector for mobilizing the resources in the  
sports sector. The Department should also make efforts to go in for Public Private  
Partnership mode to create sports infrastructure in the country for broad -basing of  
sports and for achieving excellence in sports at National and Intern ational Levels.  
The Committee also  recommends that necessary  convergence of  Khelo India with  
the MPLADS Scheme should be expedited. 
(para 17) 
Action Taken 
The recommendation of necessary convergence of Khelo India Scheme with  
the MPLADS Scheme will be duly  examined at the time of revising the Scheme, as  
the present scheme is coming to an end by March 2020. 
It has been  further informed that the Khelo  India Scheme is  currently in  
operation till 31.03.2021. Draft EFC Memorandum for New Khelo India Scheme has  
been circulated to various Ministries/Departments vide O.M. dated 25.11.2020, 
seeking their inputs for incorporation in New Khelo India Scheme. Upon receipt of  
comments, the EFC for New Khelo India Scheme will be placed before Ministry of  
Finance for its approval and the new Scheme will be notified thereafter. 
The provision of convergence of MPLADS funds with Khelo India funding  
has been kept intact in the proposed New Khelo India Scheme as well. 
Observations/Recommendations 
That the Public Partnership mode for creating sports infrastructure in the 
country be adopted and focused strategies to rope in public-private sector as has 
been done in the State of Odisha are needed, where the State Government and  
corporate sector have come together to fund ten high performance centres like 
badminton and shooting etc. Also that the Department should motivate the States to  
replicate this appreciable example of Public Partnership in sports sector. 
(para 18) 
Action Taken 
Feasibility of incorporating suitable features of such models will be duly 
examined at the time of revising the Scheme. 
It has been further informed that under the Component of Support to National 
/ Regional / State Sports Academies of Khelo India Scheme, 232 Academies are 
accredited as of now which include 156 Non SAI Academies (54 Govt. & 102 

Private). Funding to the tune of Rs 5 Lakh per annum is provided to these academies  
for each Khelo India Athletes towards sports science, coaching, lodging and 
boarding, equipment support, competition exposure etc. As of Now 1296 Athletes 
are undergoing training in these academies. 
In addition to above recently an initiative has been undertaken to fund 500 
Private Academies through National Sports federations (NSFs). 
 
Observations/Recommendations 
That the Department, in coordination with the State Government, should 
identify private residential schools having sports infrastructure / facilities for at least  
four sports disciplines of international specified standards and  develop them under  
Khelo India scheme as Model Residential ports schools or centres of Excellence in  
sports where children are allowed to nurture and develop their talent in sports. Such  
centres may be established in every district of the country.

of revising the Scheme.

Observations/Recommendations 
That the sports should be made an integral part of our education system, as it  
will enable the system to catch the talented children at a very young age. It will also  
imbibe discipline in character and generate great leadership qualities among the  
children of the country. 
(Para 32) 
Action Taken 
a) Sports is already an integral part of the Health and Physical Education, which  
is compulsory subject for classes I to X and optional at classes XI and XII. 
b) A communication has been sent to Principal Secretary (Education) / 
Education Secretary of all the State / Union Territories on 20.02.2018  to issue 
necessary instructions to all concerned in their respective State to take appropriate  
action to accord primacy to Sports in the Schools in the concerned State/Uni on 
Territory. 
c) As per the National Curriculum Framework (NCF) - 2005, 'Sports is an 
integral part of Health & Physical Education, which is compulsory subject area from  
class I to X and optional subject at Senior Secondary stage. 
d) The CBSE has introduced a streamlined and well-designed Health and 
Physical Education in their affiliated schools, especially for students for classes IX  
and X with effect from 2018 -19 session. The Programme is compulsory for all  
affiliated schools of CBSE. 
e) NCERT has developed a detailed Guideline to introduce Sports and Physical  
Health as a subject in all school classes up to class X. These guidelines have also  
included the provision of appropriate time in school timetable for this new subject. 
Observations/Recommendations 
The Co mmittee recommends the Department to take more steps to help the  
persons with disabilities to interact with other sportspersons and encourage them to  
exchange ideas on health and fitness. This would act as a motivation to other persons  
with disabilities who are engaged in any sports related activities. It will also help in  
changing the attitude of the society towards persons with disabilities and encourage  
the society to motivate and support such sports persons. 
(Para 36) 
Action Taken 
The revamped Khelo India Scheme notified vide Gazette of India dated 
09.10.2017 inter-alia, aims to encourage and promote sports among the persons with  
disabilities from the grass root level. The revamped Khelo India Scheme notified 
vide Gazette of India dated 09.10.2017 inter-alia, aims to encourage and promote  
sports among the persons with disabilities from the grass root level. The scheme has 

a vertical “promotion of sports among persons with disabilities”, for focus on the  
subject. 
The operational guidelines on promotion of sports among person with 
disabilities had been issued on 01.11.2018 and necessary steps to implement the  
scheme are being taken through the respective organizations dealing with para 
athletes. 
Further, to promote sports among the Paralympic sportspersons, Sports 
Authority of India had established a Para Centre under its SAI Training Centre  
Scheme at SAI Regional Centre, Gandhinagar in the 2016 -2017. Accordingly, it was  
decided to identify talented Para Athletes in Athletics, Swimmi ng & Power Lifting  
and to train them on regular basis for representing the country in the international  
competition. 
The SAI Regional Centre, Gandhinagar has recently been declared as a Centre  
for Excellence for Paralympics and accordingly the sports infra structure available at  
the Regional Centre, Gandhinagar has been upgraded and made friendly for regular  
training of Para Athletes. 
Observations/Recommendations 
The Committee however, recommends that efforts should be made to organize  
International Sporting events to showcase and popularize the games like 
Kalaripayattu, Mallakhamb and Kho -Kho etc. which are also considered the source  
of modern day sports. 
(Para 38) 
Action Taken 
The following initiatives have been taken by the Government to promote the  
traditional rural and indigenous games in the country: 
(i) Mallakhamb, Kalaripayattu, Gatka and Thang -Ta are being supported under  
the vertical of „Promotion of Rural and Indigenous/Tribal Games‟ under the Khelo  
India Scheme. 
(ii) Total amount of Rs.10.85 crore have been  sanctioned for the year 2019 -20 for 
infrastructure development, equipment support, appointment of coaches, training of  
coaches and scholarships. 
(iii) Out of 335 Medal Winners of Indigenous Games, 247 athletes recommended  
by the 04 NSFs are receiving scholarships amounting to Rs.10,000/ - per month per  
athlete. 
(iv) Kho-Kho and Kabaddi disciplines were included in Khelo India Youth Games  
2020 held at Guwahati. Kabaddi discipline has been included in the first edition of  
Khelo India University Games to be hel d in Bhubaneswar from February 22nd to 1st  
March, 2020

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH 
REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE COMMITTEE 
Observations/Recommendations 
That the Department should consider to appoint an eminent sportsperson or  
sports administrator as the Chief Executive Officer in the General Council of the 
Khelo India Scheme to oversee the implementation of the scheme as he/she would 
be more sensitive to the problems and needs of the budding athletes and also act as 
an interface between the needs and aspiration of the athletes and the administrative  
system for bringing best results. 
(para 12) 
Action Taken 
The General Council of the Khelo India Scheme is a policy making body  
which will advise the mission regarding implementation of the scheme. Since the  
General Council is a committee which may hold meetings 2 or 3 times in a year,  
there may not be any requirement of full time Chief Executive Officer. The 
implementation of the scheme is being done by the Ministry and Sports Authority of  
India and General Council is not directly involved in direct impl ementation of the  
scheme. 
It was further informed that the first  meeting of General Council of Khelo  
India Scheme was held on 04.08.2020 and minutes of the meeting are at Annexure- 
A. 
Further comments of the Committee 
The Committee is not convinced by the reply of the department. The  
Committee would like to point out that Khelo India Scheme is an ambitious  
scheme of the government and the General Council is the policy making body  
for the implementation of this programme. The Committee also feels that the  
General Council should meet at least 2 to 3 times in a month to oversee the  
implementation of the scheme. The Committee further reiterates that an 
eminent sportsperson or sports administrator be appointed as the Chief 
Executive Officer in the General Council  of the Khelo India Scheme as he/she  
would be more sensitive to the problems and needs of the budding athletes and  
also act as an interface between the needs and aspiration of the athletes and the  
administrative system for bringing best results.

The vacant posts of Coaches to be filled up expeditiously if excellence in  
sports is to be achieved. Further the Country has a pool of talented and experienced  
Coaches running their own academies in some of the sports disciplines. The 
Department should endeavour to rope in such coaches for visiting other 
academies/Centres in different states to coach athletes/sportspersons.

2. Due to non-finalization of the cadre restructuring in SAI and to meet the urgent  
requirement of Coaches, the services of coaches are engaged on contractual  
basis and utilize at various centres in SAI. 
3. All most maximum vacant post of coaches falling under direct recruitment 
quota are filled either through direct recruitment or contract basis. 
4. Olympians and Para -Olympian who represented the country are given direct  
employment as coaches. Result orientated coaches are also taken on deputation  
in SAI in various schemes including NCEO. Services of coaches working in  
other department are also taken as National Coach for various National Camps. 
It has been further informed that there was a ban on promotion and regular 
appointment in SAI from 1996. Subsequently SIU report followed by ERC report  
reduced the number  of sanctioned post in  SAI at various cadre.  As a result,  no 
regular recruitment could take place till 2010 since the additional posts were 
adjusted against the vacancies and the promotions were carried out with the 
condition of  restricting the strength  specified by the ERC.  Due to  the delay  in 
promotion, the coaches have not completed the required qualifying service for 
promotion to higher grade resulting in vacancy in the higher grade. However, 
promotion is already carried out by giving relaxation for qualifying service within 
the RRs wherever possible. In view of the large number of vacancies due to reason  
explained above, it has been decided to fill all vacant posts through contract by  
amending the RRs suitably to ensure adequate availa bility of coaches. Accordingly a  
proposal is being moved. Further, in order to fill the vacancy especially at the higher  
level, it is already decided to engage outstanding sportsperson / coaches working in  
other organization on deputation. It is expected t hat, the filling up of vacancies will  
be completed in six to nine months. 
In addition, Coaches are also being hired on Contract under Khelo India 
Scheme. 

Further comments of the Committee 
The Committee is not happy with the reply of the Department and would  
like to point out that out of 1524 sanctioned posts, 428 posts are still vacant. The  
Committee would like to re -emphasize that for achieving sporting excellence at  
international level, adequate facilities and focused training is necessary. The 
role of coaches in training the athletes for these events becomes very 
paramount. The Committee further points out that there are a large number of  
contract coaches in assistant coach grade. The Committee feels that the 
Department should pro vide more opportunities to these contract coaches to  
enhance their skills and make them permanent coaches against vacant posts.  
The Committee further recommends that the Department should fill the vacant  
posts of coaches so that the training of the athletes does not get affected. 
Observations/Recommendations 
That the Government should also identify new places for training in already  
existing schools, colleges and academies which have infrastructure of sports and  
hostels. These institutions should be affiliated by SAI under Khelo India Scheme 
and be provided with Coaches so that these identified sports persons can be trained  
all over India as training has far reaching impact. 
(Para 42) 
Action Taken 
The Expression of interest is open to any Institution (Educational/Sports), 
Academy or any private establishment for applying for accreditation as Khelo India  
Academy. The accredited academy will be funded as per expenditure norms. 
It was further informed that in Khelo India scheme under the vertical “Support  
to National / Regional / State Sports Academies” private sporting academies are  
accredited upon receiving expression of interest from the private academies after  
following the due process. 
Regarding details of the EoI received and action taken on them, it  was further 
informed that accreditation of academies is an ongoing process and open to all  
(Govt/Pvt) Sports academies. As on date, a total of 171 EOI applications received  
from various academies for accreditation, out of which 103 academies have been  
accredited after a due process of accreditation. 
Further comments of the Committee 
The Committee notes the steps taken by the Department to make schools,  
colleges and academies having infrastructure of sports and hostels apply for  
accreditation as Khelo  India Academy. The Committee would however, like to  
point out that under this Scheme the Department should have a robust 
monitoring mechanism for funding such academies and adequate provisions  
should be made to make them accountable financially.

The Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports met at 11.00 A.M. 
on Wednessday, the 23rd December, 2020 in Committee Room 'A', Parliament House

At the outset, the Chairman, welcomed the members of the Committee and informed them 
that the meeting had been called to consider and adopt the following draft reports: 
(i) No. 317 on the subject "Preparation for Olympics - 2021" 
(ii) No. 318 reg ATR on 311th Report on Khelo India Scheme; 
(iii) No. 319 reg ATR on 315th Report on Demands for Grants 2020-21 (Demand No. 101) of 
the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports. 

2. Thereafter, the convener of the Sub Committee made a power -point presentation to the  
Committee on the draft 317th Report on Preparations for Olympics-2021and informed that they had 
made 48 recommendations under 11 headings for short, medium and long term action plan to lay a  
road map for increasing India's medal tally in the coming Olympics. The Committee then 
discussed the draft report and adopted it. 
 
 
3. The Committee then took up for discussion the draft 318th & 319th Reports and adopted  
them after some discussion. 
4. The Committee keeping in view the fact that only  a few months were remaining for the  
Olympics authorized the Chairman, to present the Reports to the Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha 
in the inter -session period so that the Ministry can take action on the recommendations of the  
Committee. Concluding the meeting, the Chairman sought suggestions on  the subjects to be taken  
up for consideration and asked them to send them by e-mail. 
 
5. The meeting then adjourned at 12.20 P.M.

Department of Sports 
Budgetary Allocation 
Observations/Recommendations. 
1. The Committee notes that Lakshmibai National Institute of Physical Education, 
Gwalior has been given Rs.55.00 crore in BE 2020 -21 i.e. and enhancement of Rs5.00 crore 
(10%) from Rs.50.00 crore in RE 2019 -20. The Committee notes the role played by LNIPE, 
Gwalior in promoting the programmes of Physical Education and Sports in the country and 
suggests that efforts may be made by the Ministry to help the Institute for preparing aspirants 
desiring to excel in the field of Sports at National and International level. 
(Para-5.3) 
Action Taken 
The observations of Committee have been  noted for compliance. It is mentioned here that 
under able guidance of this Ministry, LNIPE, Gwalior has become an important institute in 
the field of Physical Education and Sports over the years. It became a “deemed University” in 
1995 and it has an off -campus in North East Regional Centre at Guwahati (Assam). LNIPE 
has achieved many successes in recent past. The Institute was accredited by A++ with CGPA 
of 3.79 by the National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) in 2017 and it has 
been graded as category –I deemed to be University by University grants commission (UGC) 
in 2018. The students strength of the institute was around 1400 during academic session 
2019-20.The institute has experienced faculties who run various courses at UG / PG / 
Diploma in the field of Physical Education and Sports. All the requirement of funds of the 
institutes is met by the Ministry through grant in aid which is released to them based on their 
requisition from time to time. It is expected that LNIPE being an Autonomous b ody to 
generate revenue manage its expenses in long run. 
 
Observations/Recommendations 
2. The Committee is of the view that National Sports Federations (NSFs) play an 
important functions relating in promotion and development of various Sports at national a nd 
international level. The committee finds that the allocation for assistance to various 
federation has been reduced from Rs.300.85 crore in RE2019 -20 to Rs.245.00 crore in 
BE2020-21 and it must be ensured that the decrease in allocation does not impact t he 
activities being performed by various federation. The committee feels that the Department 
should judiciously utilize the allocation and organize more and more events as they help in 
identifying talent. 
(Para-9.8) 
Action Taken 
Budgetary allocation of Rs. 245 crore for FY 2020 -21 for scheme of Assistance to NSFs is 
adequate and sufficient for preparation and training of Indian athletes and teams. If required 
the Ministry will seek additional funds at RE stage. Further expenses on training of elite 
athletes for their customized training are being taken care of under Target Olympic Podium 
(TOP) Scheme under the ambit of National sports Development Fund. The funds will not be a 
constraint for Indian athletes preparing for participation in international sports e vents 
including forthcoming Olympic Games. 
Observations/Recommendations 

 
3. The Committee also notes that despite various codes and guidelines being in place, all 
is not well in respect of functioning of NSFs, which adversely affects sportspersons and 
eventually the sports. The Committee recommends that regular elections should be held and 
the Federations function towards promotion of sports. The Committee further recommends 
that the functioning of the Federations should be regularly monitored and audited to  ensure 
that they stay corruption free and act impartially for promoting sports. 
(Para-9.9) 
Action Taken 
The Government insists upon holding of elections on regular basis by the recognised NSFs as 
per the Model election guidelines issued by the Government.  It is incumbent upon the NSFs 
to hold elections regularly and before the expiry of the tenure of existing office bearers. 
Instructions in this regard have been issued to NSFs from time to time. 
From the year 2010, the Government has introduced a system of  annual recognition 
procedure for the NSFs, under which recognition is granted to NSFs on year to year basis. 
The annual recognition of the NSFs, which fail to comply with the Government guidelines, 
are not renewed making them ineligible to receive assista nce from the Government under 
various schemes. The accounts of the NSFs are to be audited by the Chartered Accountants, 
who are in the panel of Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG). Also, the NSFs 
receiving grants of Rs. 1.00 crore or more are subject to the audit by C&AG. 
In case of failure by any NSF to adhere to the guidelines issued by the Ministry from time to 
time, appropriate action against such NSFs are taken by the Ministry which include 
suspension / de -recognition / non -renewal of annua l recognition, etc. Also, whenever a case 
of any gross irregularity in an NSF is brought to notice, action as per rules is taken by the 
Government. 
Observations/Recommendations

Department of Youth Affairs 
Observations/Recommendations 
1. The Committee feels that the Youth of the country play a very vital role and gain 
valuable experience for their future while working as volunteers. The Committee feels that 
there is steep cut in BE 2020 -21 for National Youth Corps as  Rs.90 crore have been given 
against projected demand of Rs.300.50 crore which needs to be enhanced and recommends 
that the Department should seek appropriate allocation for increasing the number of 
volunteers. 
(Para-5.6) 
Action Taken 
As far as NYC Scheme is concerned, a demand of Rs.300.50 crore was made in BE 2020 -21 
with the proposal for deployment of 15000 volunteers with monthly honorarium of 
Rs.15000/- per volunteer and the cost of volunteers training and administrative expenses. The 
enhancement of nu mber of volunteers was proposed due to the proposal of deployment of 
additional one volunteer in each 1115 blocks of 115 aspirational districts as well. 
However, budgetary provision has been made in BE 2020 -21 only for Rs.90.00 crore i.e. for 
deployment of  13251 volunteers with monthly honorarium of Rs.5000/ - and the cost of 
volunteers training and administrative expenses. Additional Fund, if required, will be sought 
at RE stage. 
Thereafter, it was further clarified that the role of National Youth Corps, co mprising of about 
13000 national youth volunteers deployed in approximately 6500 blocks of the country has 
been extremely commendable at all times.  Most of the flagship programmes of the 
Government of India especially Swachch Bharat Mission, Jal Shakti Ab hiyaan, PoshanMaah, 
Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan, Ek Bharat Shresht Bharat, Fit India etc.  are being 
implemented through the volunteers of NYKS.  During Covid-19 pandemic situation, the role 
of NYVs and about 36.79 lakhs volunteers of NYKS  has been a matte r of appreciation at 
every level.  Almost all the Hon‟ble Governors and Hon‟ble Chief Ministers and Hon‟ble 
Ministers of different States have placed their appreciation on record about the role played by 
them.  Hon‟ble Prime Minister has also praised these  volunteers in his Mann Ki Baat and 
other forums.  Earlier, the honorarium paid to NYVs till 2016 was only Rs. 2500 per month.  
After a lot of persuasion, it was enhanced to Rs. 5000/ - per month within the overall 
budgetary constraints. As stated above, th is does not commensurate with the prescribed 
remuneration for such level of people.  Hence, it is to be appreciated that in order to enlist 
their services in a much more gainful manner, their honorarium should be at par with 
minimum wages being paid in the  Government sector.  Hence it has been proposed to be 
enhanced to Rs. 15000/-

Action Taken 
SAI is establishing 23 National Centres of Excellence (NCOE) across the country to impart 
specialized training to promising athletes by providing state of the art infrastructure and

and overall supervision under the best coaches, qualified support staff and High Perfo rmance

equipment and scientific back up along with specialized training. The tr ainees are provided 
upgraded boarding and lodging facilities, sports kit, sports equipment, competition exposure, 
insurance, medical expenses etc. as per norms. 
Observations/Recommendations 
4. The Committee notes with concern the rise in number of positive  cases over the years 
and recommends that Awareness Program against doping may be run throughout the country 
vigorously to eradicate this menace. 
(Para-6.3) 
Action Taken 
With regard to anti doping awareness program, NADA is running extensive awareness 
program on anti doping in sports in country by way of disseminating information amongst 
sportspersons, educating the sportspersons, coaches and support personnel on the ill effects of 
doping through training sessions / seminars / workshops. 
To further increase  the awareness-cum-outreach level of this anti doping campaign, NADA 
has launched Mass Athlete Awareness Program Against Doping. Under this program, NADA 
is conducting numerous workshops, educational and awareness programs about the 
prohibited drugs/substa nces and methods in sports across the country for sports persons, 
young athletes, coaches and supporting staff. During the year 2019, NADA conducted 96 
such awareness programs and workshops at various places all over India in comparison to 84 
sessions in 2018, and 64 sessions in 2017. 
In addition, for the purpose of enhancing the anti doping awareness campaign and outreach, 
NADA is considering to empanel educational partners to strengthen the anti doping 
awareness activities throughout the country. 
Moreover, during the Covid restriction, online anti doping education program is being 
organized. While awareness programs have resulted in decrease in the incidence of doping in 
random sampling of sportspersons, the increase in number of positive cases is due to effective 
test distribution planning, risk assessment and sports specific dope testing/ analysis. 
Observations/Recommendations 
5. The Committee observes that while NDTL is performing its duties well, it feels that 
one Dope Testing Lab in a country having a population of 130 crore people is not sufficient 
and suggests that it may be considered to be raised to two. 
The Committee recommends that the IRMS system of NDTL, New Delhi should be urgently 
upgraded so as to ensure that the testing standards of our lab remain at par with international 
standards. The Committee hopes that the NDTL will keep on maintaining its standard and 
impartiality on Dope Test as per international norm. 
(Para-7.2) 

 
Action Taken 
Being one of 32 WADA accredited labs of the world, NDTL has  sufficient capacity to cater 
the dope testing requirement of not only our country but also our neighbouring countries. 
Hence presently the proposal for opening of 2nd Lab is not under consideration. 
NDTL has procured one more new Gas Chromatograph / Combu stion / Isotope Ratio Mass 
Spectrometry (GC/C/IRMS) System in June 2020. This system will be used to differentiate 
the origin of endogenous / exogenous origin of steroids in doping analysis, and, in the 
process, the capacity of lab for testing and quality analyses under IRMS will be substantially 
enhanced for meeting all international standards. 
NDTL has also decided to impart training to its Scientists / Staff of the lab by inviting the 
Global / Subject Experts of other WADA accredited Laboratories on the various subjects 
pertaining to functioning of the lab for its capacity building and to establish the best methods 
and practices at par with international standards. 
 
Observations/Recommendations

3. The Committee observes that out of Rs.166.55 crore allocated for National Service 
Scheme in RE -2019-20, Rs.142.12 crore has been spent which is 85.33%. The Committee 
notes that the Department has been allotted Rs.172 crore in BE 2020 -21 and hopes that the 
enhanced allocation would help the Department in increasing the number of NSS volunteers. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should encourage State Governments to set up 
more NSS units and help them suitably. The Committee also notes that there is a shortage of 
50% in the existing strength of NSS i.e. against a sanctioned strength of 199, only 98 are  
existing and recommends that the vacancies may be filled up expeditiously as they adversely 
affect the functioning. The Committee further recommends that additional funds may be 
requested for running the programmes at RE stage. 
(Para-10.7) 
Action Taken 
National Service Scheme (NSS) had received Rs.166.55 Crore in 2019 -20 in RE Stage. 
However, the total budget received in RE Stage for NSS could not be released due to 
announcement of the complete lockdown by the Government in the last week of March. 
Further, in the current financial year 2020-21 the total budget allocated in BE stage is Rs.172 
Crore. In various stakeholder consultation there has been a consistent demand for opening of 
New NSS Units. At present, the proposal for opening of more than 4000 units  
(4000x100=4,00,000) comprising 4 Lakh volunteers is under consideration in the Ministry. 
It was stated that NSS is a Centrally Sector Scheme.  The total budget allocated to NSS in BE 
2020-21 was Rs. 172 crores.  However, in RE 2020 -21, it has been brought  down to 74.33 
crores.     In the absence of adequate budget, the opening of new NSS units and enlisting of 
more NSS volunteers would be very difficult to achieve.  
National service scheme is constructed to linkage of expenditure per volunteer. Hence growth 
of Scheme is directly proportional to allocation under the scheme. In order to boost growth 
and tap into potential demand for the scheme the Department of Youth Affairs encourages 
educational institutions to organize under SFUs (Self Financing Units). Cu rrently, with these 
efforts over the years NSS has a volunteer base of 36 lakh in government financed units and 4 
lakh in self financing unit with constant efforts to grow further.

Shillong and ITBP Public School, Dwarka, Delhi have also been adopted under Khelo India 
Scheme and support will be extended as per norms

The Committee recommends  that the Department should intensify its efforts for  
broadcasting of sport talent and  should also take all measures to ensure that the 
athletes do not suffer due to the lack of funds. All efforts should be put i n place to 
facilitate the sportspersons to stay competitive so that they can win medals for the 
country in the different events lined up in the near future. Further,  more efforts be 
made for associating the corporate sector for creating sports infrastructure and training 
athletes.

join the academics due to lack of adequate education facilities, adequate financial support etc. 
and feels that whi le the country had no dearth of sporting talent, but the desired level of 
support needed to encourage the players was lacking. The Committee recommends that the 
issue needs serious consideration and needs to be resolved at the earliest to win more medals 
and reach the higher goal of being in the list of top ten performing countries in sports. 
(Para-3.10) 
 
 
  

 
 
 
Action Taken 
Under Khelo India, talent selected gets financial support of Rs. 6,28,400/ - per year. In this 
regard the selected trainees are regularly  contacted through SAI Call center to convincing 
them to join accredited academy by next academic session. Further with the help of NSFs the

Training Centres (STC), Army Boys Sports Companies (ABSC) as Residential scheme and

scheme is reviewed and enhancement is made from time to time.

The Committee notes the steps taken by the Department to motivate the budding 
sports- persons to join the academics. The Committee recommends that the Department 
should take a feedback from the sportspersons who do not join the academics to 
ascertain the reasons for the same and devise suitable intervention strategies to attract 
these sports persons to the academics accordingly. 
Observations/Recommendations 
3. The Committee observes that Netaji Subhash Institute of Sports Science, Patiala is 
playing very important role in training the sports professionals, conducting research in sports 
and sports sciences, providing coaching to sportspersons in various disciplines and giving 
scientific sup port to elite sportspersons. The Committee feels that in modern times for

parts of the country.

recommend that the Department should explore the feasibility of setting up such centres

PREFACE

I, the Chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee on its behalf, present this Thirty-
second Report of the Committee on the Maulana Azad National Urdu University Bill, 1995.

2. The.Maulana Azad National Urdu University Bill, which was introduced in the Rajya
Sabha on the 24th August, 1995, seeks to establish and incorporate a University at the
national level mainly to promote and develop Urdu language and to impart vocational and
technical education in Urdu medium through conventional teaching and distance education
system and to provide for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

3. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred the Bill to the Committee for examination
and report.

4. A Press Communique inviting suggestionsViews from individuals, organisations and
institutions interested in the subject matter of the Bill was issued on the 4th September,
1995. Several memoranda containing viewspinions in response thereto were received by the
Committee.

5. The Committee considered the Bill in four sittings and heard the oral evidence of
some of the members of the Expert Committee which recommended to set up an Urdu
University.

6. The Committee, in its meeting held on December 8, 1995, considered the draft report
on the Bill and adopted the same for presentation/laying in both the Houses of Parliament.

New De ui, 2. UPENDRA
December 8, 1995 Chairman,

17 Agrahayana, 1917 (Saka) Committee on Human Resource Development.

(iii)



REPORT

The National Policy on Education (NPE) emphasises that the minority groups, which
are educationally backward, need greater attention in regard to educational facilities, in the
interest of equality and social justice. The NPE also reiterates the recommendation of the
Kothari Commission that University education should be imparted in the regional languages.
In order to implement various postulates of the NPE, 22 Task Forces on different subject
areas were constituted by the Department of Education in the Ministry of Human Resource
Development to develop Programme of Action (POA), which was presented to Parliament.
The Task Force on Minority Education, headed by Shri Aziz Qureshi, recommended the
setting up of an Urdu University. To give effect to this recommendation, the Government
constituted * an Expert Committee which was, again, headed by
Shri Aziz Qureshi to examine and recommend the form and content of such a University.
The Committee submitted its report to the Government in June, 1993. The Bill, under the
consideration of the Committee, has been drafted in the wake of the Qureshi Committee's
report.

2. Urdu is one of the richest and most powerful languages, born in India as a result of
the constant interaction between the Persian language and a variety of Indian languages. It
has, in fact, remained one of the commonly spoken languages in India for centuries
together, the lingua franca of not only the North Indian and Dakkhani Muslims but of many
from other communities too. Indeed, Urdu was being used as a medium of instruction for
engineering and medical courses even in the nineteenth century. But, regrettably, with the
passage of time, Urdu has got relegated to the background in India’s educational and
cultural scene, in spite of the fact that Urdu is the mother tongue of a large number of
Indians. The root cause for this appears to be the special position Urdu occupies in the
linguistic map of India. For although Urdu-speaking people are distributed all ovet the
country, Urdu is not the primary language in any one or more States of the Union. In such a
situation, the responsibility for the promotion and development of the Urdu language falls
on the Central Government, as confirmed by the Department of Education, Ministry of
Human Resource Development. Hence, the need for an Urdu University at the national
level.

3. The Committee has been informed that the proposed University would concentrate
on higher education through the medium of Urdu. It would also impart education and
training in vocational and technical subjects to develop skills, particularly of women, who are
not able to prosecute their studies in the conventional institutions adequately due to social
reasons. That is why the mode of distance education had been suggested by the Qureshi
Committee for this University. It has been decided that the Urdu University will use the
material and facilities of the Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU), as far as
possible, and will avoid creating parallel arrangements for the production of material and
audio-visual programmes. These decisions have been welcomed by the Committee.

4. The Department of Education has stated that the Expert Committee, set up for the
purpose, had envisaged a very large brief for the University, including powers of affiliation.
The Department thought that one institution would not be able to solve all the problems;
rather, it should concern itself with matters or subjects it can handle efficiently. Otherwise, it
might prove to be counter-productive. In this perspective, it was felt by the Department that
in the main campus the Urdu University should concentrate on vocational/Janguage
education. In other disciplines, it should reach out to the rest of the country, and if
necessary abroad, through distance education. The proposed University would be a single
campus University with no provision for affiliation. It would offer an opportunity to Urdu-

1



2

knowing people to prosecute higher education in that language and use Urdu as a vehicle
of science and technology, commerce and social sciences. These clarifications were
welcomed by the Committee.

5. Currently, Urdu is being taught in 43 Universities, but in no University it is a
medium of instruction, except in courses in Unani medicine and certain classical
languages. Besides imparting education and training in vocational and technical subjects
through the Urdu medium, the University would also provide wider access to people
willing to pursue higher education and training in the Urdu medium. The proposed
University would, therefore, teach other general subjects also and make appropriate
arrangements to adopt enough study material in Urdu language for technical subjects.

6. During the course of evidence, members of the Expert Committee, which
recommended setting up of the Urdu University, protested that some of their main
recommendations did not find place in the Bill, ‘‘perhaps because”, as they put it ‘the
report of the Committee was examined in the UGC and the Ministry of Human
Resource Development by the people who were not very conversant with the position of
Urdu and the objectives of establishing an Urdu University”. As any amendments at this
stage would take a long time, they suggested that the Bill might be passed so that the
process of setting up the University was not further delayed. The Committee trusts that
the Governing Body of the University would bear in mind all relevant suggestions of the
Expert Committee while finalising the courses in the new University.

7. Members of the Standing Committee on HRD appreciated the laudable objectives
sought to be achieved by setting up of an Urdu University. It was generally agreed that
this long delayed measure would prove fully effective only if it was conceived as a part
of a larger endeavour to restore Urdu to its due place in society by expansion of Urdu
education at the school level, specially for elementary education, and the provision of
adequate employment opportunities for graduates passing out in the Urdu medium.

8. Some members felt that if the said objectives could be achieved by strengthening
and developing the Urdu departments in the existing Universities or by creating a
separate wing for teaching in Urdu medium in the Indira Gandhi National Open
University or by setting up an institutecentre without giving it the form of a University.
They also argued that instead of spending a huge amount of money on establishing a
separate University for Urdu, the same could be distributed to various Universities and
institutions so as to enable them to achieve the objectives contained in the Urdu
University Bill. This would, they felt, facilitate decentralisation of infrastructure to
different corners of the country, instead of concentrated at one place. Other Members
were of the view that for improving the facilities for teaching the Urdu language need to
be improved. The establishment of such a University would be an important step towards
evolving an integrated strategy for the restoration of Urdu to its deserved place in
contemporary India

9. As regards developing Urdu through the existing departments/institutions in
certain Universities, rather than setting up a University exclusively for this purpose, it
was clarified by the Ministry of HRD that the Departments of Urdu ‘in the existing
Universities were mainly concentrating on literature and the emphasis, by and large, was
confined mainly to writingteaching literary critics, fiction, poetry, etc. Besides, almost all
the existing Universities and Colleges provide teaching in media other than Urdu. There
is a sizeable section of Urdu-speaking people whose needs require to be met through a
University like the proposed one. With the distance education mode, the reach-out of the



3

University would be at the all India level, which would give opportunity to Urdu-speaking
people, particularly women, to pursue higherVocational education and training through the
medium of Urdu.

10. Regarding the suggestion for a separate wing for Urdu in IGNOU, the
representative of the Department of Education submitted before the Committee that
IGNOU had not been able to fulfil, so far, its mandate in English and Hindi. It has to fulfil
mandate first before it can take up another language.

11. Some Members of the Committee expressed their apprehension about the ‘job
prospects of students, trained particularly in technical and vocational subjects through the
medium of Urdu. Other Members stressed the importance of integrating University level
education with job opportunities in different sectors and that incentives should be provided
for availing of the new educational opportunities offered by the Urdu University. It was
contended by the Department that students coming out of this University would have no
problem in the job market as a majority of them were expected to be absorbed in self-
employment. It was argued that keeping in view the advantages of prosecuting higher studies
in regional languages, students would acquire greater proficiency in subjects they study in

, Urdu medium thereby improving their prospects for employment.

12. About the financial requirement, the Department stated that a sum of Rs. 6.00
crores (Approx.) will be required in the first three years till such time as land becomes
available and the construction programme begins in a regular manner and sizeable
recruitment of the faculty is made and courses are started. This amount does not include
provision for equipment etc. After three years, the University would require about Rs. 3-5
crores per year for non-recurring items and an equal amount for recurring expenditure.

13. When asked whether the UGC has got any assurance from the Department of
Education for additional resources, the Chairman, UGC, said that they had been assured
that these would be made available by the Government. The Committee recommends that
additional resources should be made available for this University.

14. As regards watering down the recommendations of the Qureshi Committee in the
Bill, the representative of the Department of Education, accepted that the Bill was “not the
exact reproduction of all the recommendations made by that Committee”. The Bill, in fact,
was drafted after taking those recommendations into serious consideration.

He stated:

“this is a small but an important gesture towards the legitimate demand of a sizeable
number of people. This may not meet all their hopes and aspirations; but it, no doubt, is a
significant step towards that end.”

15. In view of the nature of the distribution of the Urdu-speaking people in the country
and the Central Government’s commitment to help educationally backward minority groups
and also keeping in mind the long-standing demand for teaching technical subjects through
Urdu medium in an open University system, the Committee recommends that the Bill be
adopted, subject to the observations made by it in the preceding paragraphs. The Committee
also hopes, that the new University would be brought into existance by the time the nai’ था
celebrates the 500 anniversary of its independence.



PRESS RELEASE

The Maulana Azad National Urdu University Bill, 1995, was introduced in the Rajya
Sabha on the 24th August, 1995. This Bilf has been referred to the Parliamentary Standing

examination and report.
